text: A typhoon passes and leaves an egg the size of a house on the sand, and the first men to reach it start pricing tickets. Ishirō Honda's 1964 film gives the discovery to entrepreneurs rather than scientists, and gives the objection to two reporters who keep asking who the egg belongs to. The answer arrives as two very small women from Infant Island, and what follows is an actual negotiation — salvage rights, ownership, what neighbours owe each other — argued in offices while something stirs in the water near Nagoya. Eighty-nine minutes allows no stalling. The structure is a sequence of refusals: the egg is not returned, the plea is turned down, and then Japan has to ask Infant Island for help anyway. Honda films the storm's wreckage and the wreckage that comes after it in the same tone.

The most demanding role in the film is the one played at dinner: a perfumed idler with no opinions about anything. Rouben Mamoulian sends a nobleman's son home to California in 1820 to find the place under a dictatorship, and the answer the son settles on is to be insufferable in public, fussing with a handkerchief in rooms full of armed men. The night rides are the easier half of the job. Drawing rooms get the same attention here as duels, because the sustained strain is conversational — whether an act of uselessness can be held at a family table, week after week, in front of people who would rather believe it. Ninety-four minutes, almost none of it spent explaining itself. When the swordplay finally moves indoors and close, it settles accounts that small talk has been running up for an hour.

A fugitive hides in the one workplace where a body falling from a great height is on the schedule. Richard Rush drops a man wanted by the police into a job that has just come open on a film set, so his cover now depends on a director who needs him to fall, repeatedly, on camera. Four genres are listed for it and none of them is a hedge; the picture changes gear inside single scenes, and the gag and the threat are often the same event watched from two different chairs. Two hours and eleven minutes of a production where the footage cannot be trusted and neither can the man calling for another take. It is also attentive to the leading lady's working conditions — what is asked of her, by whom, in exchange for being looked at.

Eighteen years in Folsom, and the operation run from inside is steadier than anything the street ever offered. Edward James Olmos films both halves of Santana's life as one administration: the block has meetings, accounts and enforcement, and when release comes the organisation does not stop needing its manager. The National Film Registry holds it. Olmos is patient about how clerical violence becomes once an institution stands behind it, and he declines the scene in which a man announces that he has changed and is believed. The intention to live quietly reads, among the people waiting for him, as a request nobody has a procedure for. The neighbourhood stays specific — same corners, eighteen years on — and the old friends are allowed to make their case in their own terms.

The extortion is small: lunch money, collected daily, from boys who find paying cheaper than the alternative. Tony Bill's 1980 film treats a high-school corridor as a market, and Clifford's innovation is to buy a deterrent rather than throw a punch — a large, silent classmate whose reputation has grown monstrous and whose actual circumstances turn out to be sadder than the stories. Early on the comedy comes from how businesslike it all is: a hired presence, a fee, terms. Then it stops being businesslike, because the hired presence has a history of his own to survive. Ninety-six minutes, and the film keeps in view that the boy running the protection racket is the same age as his customers and is building something out of it.

The savings are the whole of it: a secretary from Ohio has paid for this trip herself and will not admit to being lonely in the middle of it. David Lean's Venice is a working city of stone stairs, rented rooms and small transactions, not a backdrop, and for a long early stretch the film is a woman eating alone in public, managing her own camera, her drink, the attention of strangers. She is middle-aged, and the film says so plainly. Then there is Renato Di Rossi, elegant, quick, an offer in himself. What a summer costs and what it buys are asked here as literal questions: how many days are left, what a holiday can be made to carry, when the ticket home is dated. One hundred minutes, and it counts them.

The basement is a film studio and a torture chamber at once, and the man who fitted it out sees no contradiction: evidence has to be recorded. Jang Joon-hwan gives his hero a theory — that the country's leaders are reptiles sent here to take the place over — and then gives him one of those leaders, tied up and entirely able to argue back. KOFA counts it among a hundred Korean films. Slapstick in a very unpleasant room: a homemade rig, a camera running, a joke timed to land a beat after something has actually hurt. The film refuses to settle into a register, so a gag arrives and the next shot asks to be believed. Two hours of that would collapse if it were not careful about how this particular man reached this particular theory.

Arthur Simon Simpson is a bad thief, which is exactly why better thieves have a use for him. Jules Dassin puts the swindle in Greece and the theft in Istanbul, where a dagger crusted with emeralds sits under glass in the Topkapi Museum, and then hands a plan explained in exhaustive detail to the least reliable man available. This is a caper in daylight and colour, tourists everywhere, the rehearsals played for laughs and the museum floor treated as arithmetic: weight, alarm, the distance a rope has to cover. Two hours is long for the form, and the extra time goes into how little the crew like one another. Simpson spends most of it being flattered by people who need him hopeful, half-understanding what he has agreed to.

Seven minutes to stage a Wagner opera, costume changes and all, with a hunting rifle in it. Chuck Jones takes the oldest routine on the lot — a man with a gun, a rabbit who declines to be shot — and drops it into Siegfried, Elmer Fudd promoted to hero, Bugs Bunny cast as Brunnhilde. The National Film Registry keeps it. The music is played straight, or straight enough, and the drawing answers it: shadows falling like stage light, skies that behave like painted cloth, a spear carried as though it weighed something. What a feature would spend an hour establishing is done in a held pose and a cut. Both performers eat the scenery on the way through, and neither winks at the size of what is being attempted.

The uranium mine is a fake, and the fake is not the story; the story is the waiting around. John Huston shot this in Italy, in English, with a small company of swindlers stalled in transit and nothing to do except work on each other, and the National Board of Review named it among the year's ten best, an odd fate for a film so uninterested in its own plot. Ninety-five minutes in which the mine is barely mentioned twice in a row. Talk is the whole enterprise: credentials politely exchanged, loyalties miscounted, a shared willingness to commit crimes discussed as a matter of taste. Not a thriller loosening into comedy, but a comedy that never meant to tighten, played by people who seem to find their own scheme faintly tedious.

Most of the film is committee work: representatives in Philadelphia arguing over the wording of rules that do not exist yet. Peter H. Hunt keeps the drama procedural — motions, delays, who is in the room and who has gone home — and puts at its centre a writing assignment nobody wants. Benjamin Franklin and John Adams hand it to Thomas Jefferson: draft the statement that tells Britain the colonies are finished with it. That task is the smallest thing in the room and the only one that will outlast the room. Made in 1972, the film is content to let the founding be clerical, cramped and transactional, argued by men who each want something in exchange. Two and a half hours of talk, and the pull is watching a sentence assembled by negotiation instead of inspiration.

He finds out he can sing while serving a manslaughter sentence, and the film treats that as a fact rather than a redemption. Richard Thorpe's 1957 picture keeps the prison stretch hard and unsentimental, then follows the release into the record business and shoots that as another set of arrangements to be worked: contracts, percentages, whose name ends up on a song. The National Film Registry holds it. What stays odd is Vince Everett's manner — he arrives at success already hardened, handles affection as though it were a trade, and the film lets him be unpleasant for long stretches without hurrying to correct him. Ninety-six minutes, and the numbers are staged as labour: a man at work in a studio, on a stage, in front of people who are paid to be there.

A giant sea snail is the object of the search, and the film spends two and a half hours going after it. Richard Fleischer starts with a village veterinarian who talks with animals and moves him outward in stages — surgery, then ship, then places off the chart — with live creatures crowded into nearly every frame, a logistical problem the camera has to solve in the open, take after take. The scale is intermission scale: songs delivered to livestock, horizons built rather than found, an orchestra behind all of it. Family fantasy of this period usually keeps its animals drawn; here an animal has to hit a mark on cue. Strain and pleasure turn out to be the same thing, an enormous apparatus built around a modest proposition about preferring animals to neighbours.

The counterattack on the new teacher comes as rumour and paperwork at least as often as it comes as fists. Richard Brooks gives half the film to the staffroom of North Manual High: colleagues who gave up years ago and resent a man who hasn't, an administration that prefers its trouble unreported. Richard Dadier keeps trying methods — attention, curiosity, anything that holds a room for ten minutes — while the boys operate on the correct assumption that a teacher's authority is mostly performance. Black and white, 101 minutes, and the class is never filmed as one mass; several of them are running private calculations about what school is worth and how soon they can leave. The violence, when it arrives, is almost administrative in its patience.
